answer: We obtain \(\displaystyle\int_a^b |f_n(x)-f(x)|\,dx \le \int_a^b \varepsilon\,dx = \varepsilon(b-a)\). The bound \(\varepsilon\) appears because the integrand \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\) is uniformly bounded by \(\varepsilon\) on the entire interval, so the integral is at most \(\varepsilon\) times the length of the interval.

question: From the definition of uniform absolute‑convergence, explain why the existence of a single \(m\) that works for all \(x\) in the domain is crucial, and how this contrasts with the pointwise convergence condition that would allow \(m\) to depend on \(x\).
answer: Uniform absolute‑convergence requires that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists an \(m\) such that for all \(n\ge m\) and for all \(x\) in the domain, \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\). This single \(m\) works uniformly over the whole domain, guaranteeing that the convergence does not depend on the particular point \(x\). In contrast, pointwise convergence would allow a different \(m_x\) for each \(x\), so the bound might fail to hold uniformly across the domain.

question: Combining the uniform bound \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) for all \(x\) with the triangle inequality for integrals, explain why the sequence of integrals \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx\) converges to \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\), and what role the absolute value plays in this argument.
answer: Because \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) uniformly, we have \(\displaystyle\int_a^b |f_n(x)-f(x)|\,dx < \varepsilon(b-a)\). By the triangle inequality for integrals, \(\displaystyle\bigl|\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx - \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\bigr| \le \int_a^b |f_n(x)-f(x)|\,dx\). question: Suppose \((f_n)\) is a sequence of continuous functions on \([a,b]\) that converges uniformly to \(f\). Additionally, the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(f_{n+1}-f_n)\) converges uniformly absolutely. answer: Uniform absolute convergence of the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(f_{n+1}-f_n)\) implies that the sequence of partial sums \(S_N(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}(f_{n+1}-f_n)=f_{N+1}(x)-f_1(x)\) converges uniformly to a continuous function \(S(x)=f(x)-f_1(x)\). Hence \(f_N\) converges uniformly to \(f\). By the uniform limit theorem, \(f\) is continuous. For each \(N\), \(\int_a^b f_N(x)\,dx\) exists because \(f_N\) is continuous. Uniform convergence allows us to interchange limit and integral: \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\int_a^b f_N(x)\,dx = \int_a^b \lim_{N\to\infty} f_N(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx.\) Thus the equality holds.

Explain why pointwise convergence alone does not guarantee continuity of \(f\), and give an example that illustrates this distinction.
answer: Pointwise convergence does not control how the functions behave uniformly across the interval, so discontinuities can appear in the limit.  For example, \(f_n(x)=x^n\) on \([0,1]\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\in[0,1)\) and \(f(1)=1\), which is discontinuous at \(x=1\).  Uniform convergence would have prevented this jump.

question: In the lecture, it was shown that if a sequence of functions \(f_n\) converges uniformly to \(f\) on \([a,b]\), then \(\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). Explain why the uniform convergence condition is essential for this conclusion and how the uniform limit theorem guarantees the interchange of limit and integral.
answer: Uniform convergence guarantees that for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(N\) such that \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon/(b-a)\) for all \(x\in[a,b]\) and \(n\ge N\). Integrating this inequality yields \(\bigl|\int_a^b f_n-\int_a^b f\bigr|\le(b-a)\sup_{x}|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\). Thus the sequence of integrals converges to the integral of the limit, and the uniform limit theorem provides the bound that allows the limit and integral to be interchanged.

Using the uniform limit theorem, explain why a uniformly absolutely convergent series of continuous functions has a continuous sum, and discuss why uniform absolute‑convergence is a stronger requirement than mere pointwise convergence.
answer: Uniform absolute‑convergence implies that \(\sum_{k}\sup_{x}|u_k(x)|<\infty\), which in particular forces \(\sum_{k}u_k(x)\) to converge uniformly. Since each partial sum is continuous, the uniform limit theorem tells us the limit function is continuous. Uniform absolute‑convergence is stronger than pointwise convergence because it controls the entire tail of the series uniformly over the domain, ensuring uniform convergence and hence continuity, whereas pointwise convergence alone does not.

question: It was discussed that if \(f_n\) are continuously differentiable, \(f_n \to f\) uniformly, and \(f_n'\to g\) uniformly, then \(f\) is differentiable with \(f'=g\). answer: By the fundamental theorem of calculus, \(f_n(x)-f_n(a)=\int_a^x f_n'(t)\,dt\). Taking limits and using the uniform limit theorem on the integrals of \(f_n'\) (which converge uniformly to \(g\)) gives \(f(x)-f(a)=\int_a^x g(t)\,dt\). Differentiating both sides shows \(f'(x)=g(x)\). Uniform convergence of the derivatives is necessary to apply the uniform limit theorem to the integrals; without it, the limit of the integrals may not equal the integral of the limit.

Taking the limit as \(\|P\|\to0\) gives \(\lim_{\|P\|\to0}S(f_n,P)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). Thus the limit of the Riemann sums of \(f_n\) equals the integral of \(f\).

answer: Uniform convergence implies that for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(N\) such that \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon/(b-a)\) for all \(x\) and \(n\ge N\). For a partition \(P\) with sufficiently small mesh, the Riemann sums satisfy \(|S(f_n,P)-S(f,P)|\le(b-a)\cdot\varepsilon/(b-a)=\varepsilon\). Hence as \(\|P\|\to0\), both \(S(f_n,P)\) and \(S(f,P)\) converge to the same limit, which is \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).

question: Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of continuous functions on \([a,b]\) that converges uniformly to \(f\). Using the discussion about limits and integrals, explain why \(\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\), and what role uniform convergence plays in justifying the interchange of limit and integral.
answer: Uniform convergence allows us to control the difference between \(f_n\) and \(f\) uniformly over the entire interval. For any \(\varepsilon>0\) choose \(N\) such that \(\sup_{x\in[a,b]}|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon/(b-a)\) for all \(n\ge N\). Then \(\bigl|\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\bigr|\le\int_a^b |f_n(x)-f(x)|\,dx\le(b-a)\sup|f_n-f|<\varepsilon\). Hence \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n=\int_a^b f\). Uniform convergence is essential because it ensures the error bound \(\sup|f_n-f|\) is small for all \(x\), allowing the interchange of limit and integral; pointwise convergence alone would not provide such a uniform bound and the interchange could fail.

answer: Because \(f_n'\) converges uniformly to \(g\), for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(N\) such that \(|f_n'(x)-g(x)|<\varepsilon\) for all \(x\in[a,b]\) and \(n\ge N\). Integrating this inequality from \(a\) to \(x\) and using the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \(|f_n(x)-f_n(a)-\int_a^x g(t)\,dt|<\varepsilon(b-a)\). Taking limits as \(n\to\infty\) and noting that \(f_n(a)\to f(a)\) yields \(f(x)-f(a)=\int_a^x g(t)\,dt\). Differentiating both sides shows \(f'(x)=g(x)\) for all \(x\).
